title: Shadows: what happens when something blocks the light

summary.text: Hold your hand in front of a torch, and a dark patch with the shape of your hand appears on the wall. That patch is a shadow. It forms because light travels in straight lines and cannot go through your hand. In this unit your child finds out what a shadow needs, which side it falls on, and why the same toy can make a tiny shadow or a giant one. They also make shadow puppets and put on a shadow play, like the puppeteers of Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Odisha.
summary.art: A girl of 7 in a dim room holding a cardboard elephant puppet on a stick in front of a phone torch, with a huge elephant shadow on the wall behind her and her little brother staring up at it.

intro.hook: Switch on a torch and hold your hand in front of it. A dark hand appears on the wall. Where did that dark hand come from?
intro.text: Hold your hand still between the torch and the wall. Now take your hand away. The dark hand is gone. Put your hand back, and it comes back. The dark hand on the wall is called a shadow. In this unit we find out what makes a shadow, and how to make one grow, shrink, split in two and tell a story.
intro.art: A child's open hand in front of a lit phone torch, and a dark hand-shaped shadow on a plain wall behind it.

outcomes: By the end I can say that a shadow forms where something blocks light.
By the end I can name the three things a shadow needs: a light, something that blocks it, and a surface for the shadow to fall on.
By the end I can show that a shadow grows when the thing moves nearer the light, and shrinks when it moves nearer the wall.
By the end I can say which side a shadow falls on: the side away from the light.
By the end I can count the shadows that two lights make, and say why there are two.
By the end I can make a shadow puppet, use it to tell a story, and name a shadow-puppet play from India.

terms.meaning: A light source is something that gives out its own light.
terms.example: The Sun, a torch, a tube light and a lit diya are light sources.
terms.art: A row of four light sources: the Sun, a torch, a tube light and a small lit diya.

terms.meaning: A shadow is the darker patch where light cannot reach, because something is in the way.
terms.example: At lunch, there is a shadow on the floor under the dining table.
terms.art: A dining table lit by a ceiling light, with a dark patch on the floor underneath it.

terms.meaning: To block light means to stop it from getting through.
terms.example: Your hand blocks the torch light, so a hand-shaped shadow appears on the wall.
terms.art: A hand in a beam of torch light, with light going round the edges and a dark patch behind the hand.

terms.meaning: An opaque thing lets no light through. Opaque things make dark shadows.
terms.example: A steel plate, a book and your hand are opaque.
terms.art: A steel plate, a book and a hand, each with a dark shadow behind it.

terms.meaning: Light goes from the torch in straight lines. It does not bend round a thing that is in its way.
terms.example: That is why your hand's shadow has the same outline as your hand.
terms.art: Straight dotted lines from a torch, passing the edges of a hand and ending at the edges of its shadow on the wall.

terms.meaning: The outline is the line all round the edge of a shape.
terms.example: A shadow shows only the outline of a thing, not its colour or its face.
terms.art: A coloured toy elephant on the left, and a plain black elephant-shaped shadow on the right that shows only the outline.

terms.meaning: A sharp shadow has a clear, crisp edge.
terms.example: Hold your hand close to the wall, and its shadow is sharp.
terms.art: A hand close to a wall with a crisp-edged shadow.

terms.meaning: A fuzzy edge is a soft, blurred edge round a shadow. Scientists call this soft edge the penumbra.
terms.example: Hold your hand close to the torch, and the edge of its shadow goes fuzzy.
terms.art: A big hand shadow with a soft grey blurry edge round the dark middle.

terms.meaning: A shadow puppet is a flat cut-out figure on a stick. You move it in front of a light, and people watch its shadow.
terms.example: A cardboard crow on an ice-cream stick makes a crow shadow on the wall.
terms.art: A cardboard crow cut-out taped to an ice-cream stick, and the crow shadow on the wall.

terms.meaning: In a shadow play, the screen is a thin white cloth or paper. The light is behind it, and the people watching sit in front.
terms.example: In Kerala, tholpavakoothu puppeteers use a long white cloth as their screen.
terms.art: A long white cloth screen glowing with lamplight from behind, with dark puppet shadows on it and people sitting in front.

explanations.context: This card is about the dark patch you see behind your hand when a torch is on.
explanations.definition: A shadow is the darker patch where light cannot reach, because something blocks it.
explanations.description: Light comes out of the torch and lands on the wall. When your hand is in the way, the light that hits your hand stops there. The part of the wall behind your hand gets no light from the torch. That part looks dark. Nothing dark comes out of your hand. The shadow is simply the place the light could not reach.
examples: A dark hand on the wall when a torch shines on your hand.
The dark patch under a table at lunch.
The cool shade under a tree or an umbrella on a sunny day.
explanations.art: A torch, a hand and a wall, with yellow light reaching the wall everywhere except behind the hand.

explanations.context: This card is about what you need to make a shadow, from the Make a Shadow, Lose a Shadow activity.
explanations.definition: To make a shadow you need a light, something that blocks the light, and a surface for the shadow to fall on.
explanations.description: Switch the torch off, and the shadow is gone. Take your hand away, and the shadow is gone. Shine the torch at an open window at night, and there is no wall for the shadow to fall on, so you see none. All three are needed at once: a light, a thing in the way, and a surface behind it.
examples: No light: switch off the torch and the hand shadow vanishes.
No blocker: take your hand away and the wall is all lit.
No surface: shine the torch out of a window into the night sky, and you see no shadow.
explanations.art: Three small pictures: a torch switched off with no shadow, a torch with no hand and a lit wall, and a torch with a hand and a dark shadow.

explanations.context: This card is about why a shadow has the same outline as the thing that makes it.
explanations.definition: Light travels in straight lines, so it cannot bend round a thing that is in its way.
explanations.description: Light from the torch goes out in straight lines in many directions. The lines that pass just by the edge of your hand go straight on to the wall. The lines that hit your hand stop. So the edge of the shadow follows the edge of your hand. That is why a shadow has the outline of the thing that made it, but no colour and no face.
examples: A shadow of a cup has the outline of the cup.
A shadow of your hand shows the gaps between your fingers.
A shadow of a fork shows each of its prongs.
explanations.art: Straight lines drawn with a ruler from a torch past the edges of a toy, meeting the edges of the toy's shadow on the wall.

explanations.context: This card is about what you found in the Near or Far test, where you moved a toy between a torch and a wall.
explanations.definition: When a thing moves nearer the light, its shadow gets bigger. When it moves nearer the wall, its shadow gets smaller, until it is about the same size as the thing.
explanations.description: Light spreads out from a torch, like a cone. Close to the torch, the cone is narrow, so a small toy blocks a big part of it. That blocked part spreads out all the way to the wall, so the shadow is big. Close to the wall, the light has already spread wide, and the toy blocks only a small part, so the shadow is small. The toy itself stays the same size the whole time.
examples: A toy about as tall as your finger made a shadow about as tall as a ruler when it was a ruler's length from the torch.
In a shadow play, a puppeteer pulls a puppet back towards the lamp to make the shadow grow huge.
explanations.art: Three pictures of the same toy between a torch and a wall: next to the wall with a small shadow, halfway with a bigger one, and next to the torch with a huge one.

explanations.context: This card is about why some shadows have a crisp edge and some have a soft one.
explanations.definition: A shadow is sharpest when the light is small and the thing is close to the surface. It gets a fuzzy edge when the light is big or the thing is close to the light.
explanations.description: A torch is not a single point. Light comes from all over its bright part. Near the edge of a shadow, your hand hides some of that bright part but not all of it. So that part of the wall gets a little light and looks grey, not dark. That grey ring is the fuzzy edge, the penumbra. A tiny phone torch makes sharper shadows than a big torch.
examples: Your hand pressed close to the wall makes a sharp shadow.
Your hand close to the torch makes a big shadow with a fuzzy edge.
On a cloudy day, the whole sky is the light, so shadows are soft or hard to see.
explanations.art: Two hand shadows side by side: one small and crisp, one big with a soft grey edge.

explanations.concept: Which side a shadow falls on
explanations.context: This card is about the Which Way Does It Point? activity, where you moved a torch round a toy.
explanations.definition: A shadow always falls on the side of the thing that is away from the light.
explanations.description: Light comes from the torch and stops at the toy. The place that misses out is behind the toy, on the far side from the torch. Move the torch to the left, and the shadow swings to the right. Lift the torch high above the toy, and the shadow becomes short and sits close round the toy's feet. If you know where a shadow is, you can work out where the light is.
examples: The torch on the left: the shadow falls on the right.
A light on the ceiling: the shadow of a chair is under the chair.
The Sun in the east in the morning: shadows point to the west.
explanations.art: A toy on a plate seen from above, with a torch on four sides in turn and the shadow pointing the opposite way each time.

explanations.context: This card is about the Two Lights test, where one toy was lit by two torches.
explanations.definition: Each light makes its own shadow of a thing. Two lights make two shadows.
explanations.description: Each torch sends its own light, and the toy blocks some light from each one. So there is one shadow for each torch. Each shadow is pale, not dark, because the other torch still lights it. Where the two shadows overlap, no light from either torch gets in, so that part is darkest. Switch one torch off, and its shadow disappears.
examples: A chair in a room with a tube light and a lamp has two shadows.
Players on a cricket ground at night often have four shadows, one from each tall tower of lights.
In a corridor with many ceiling lights, you can see a shadow of yourself under each light.
explanations.art: A toy lit by two torches from different sides, with two pale grey shadows on the wall and a darker patch where they overlap.

explanations.context: This card is about a question people have argued about for a very long time: is a shadow something, or nothing?
explanations.description: A shadow has a shape and a size. You can draw round it and measure it. Yet it is made of light that is missing. People see this in different ways.
examples: You can measure your toy's shadow with a ruler.
Switch off the light, and the shadow is gone at once, with nothing left behind.

perspectives.who: The Mohists, thinkers in China about 2,300 years ago
perspectives.explanation: A shadow is the place where light is blocked. It does not really travel along with you. Where the light comes back, the old shadow is gone, and a new one forms in the new place.
A shadow is a place that gets less light than the places round it. It is not a thing made of something, but its edge and size follow exact rules, so it can be measured.

explanations.art: A girl looking at her shadow on a wall, with three thought bubbles: a dark twin, a patch with no light, and a ruler measuring the shadow.

explanations.context: This card is about plants and animals that notice shadows and act on them.
explanations.definition: Many living beings sense shadows and change what they do.
explanations.description: A plant in the shade of other leaves senses the shade. The light under leaves has less red light, and plants feel that change. The plant then grows a longer stem to reach the sunlight. Giant clams in the sea pull in quickly when a shadow passes over them. A shadow can mean a fish is coming close. In Africa, a bird called the black heron spreads her wings into an umbrella over the water while she fishes.
examples: A tulsi plant on a crowded windowsill grows taller and thinner than one with space round them.
A pigeon on the balcony rail may fly off when your shadow falls over them.
The black heron fishes in the shade of her own wings.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how plants behave
perspectives.explanation: A plant feels shade and chooses to grow taller. Plants sense the light round them and decide how to grow.
They call the plant's growth an automatic response, set off by light-sensing parts called phytochromes.

explanations.art: Two potted tulsi plants: one on their own in the sun, short and bushy, and one crowded by bigger plants, tall and thin.

explanations.concept: Shadow puppets in India and the world
explanations.context: This card is about shadow plays, where people tell stories with shadows.
explanations.definition: A shadow play tells a story with the shadows of flat puppets, moved between a light and a screen.
explanations.description: India has many shadow plays. In Kerala, tholpavakoothu puppeteers in Palakkad work behind a long white cloth, with a row of oil lamps behind them, and tell the Ramayana over many nights. In Andhra Pradesh it is called tholu bommalata, in Karnataka togalu gombeyaata, and in Odisha ravanachhaya. The puppets are cut from leather. In 1926, a German artist called Lotte Reiniger made a whole film with shadow puppets cut from thin card, The Adventures of Prince Achmed. It is the oldest full-length animated film that still survives.
examples: Tholpavakoothu in Kerala.
Tholu bommalata in Andhra Pradesh.
Ravanachhaya in Odisha, with puppets of plain leather that make dark shadows.
Wayang kulit in Indonesia.
explanations.art: A shadow-play stage at night: a white cloth glowing from oil lamps behind it, leather puppet shadows of an elephant and a king, and people sitting on mats in front.

agreed.text: Light travels in straight lines, so a thing in its way makes a shadow with the same outline.
agreed.evidence: Every shadow you make has the outline of the thing in front of the light. Light passing through a small hole into a dark room makes a straight beam you can see in dusty air.

agreed.text: A thing makes a bigger shadow when it is nearer the light, and a smaller one when it is nearer the surface.
agreed.evidence: You can measure it with a toy, a torch and a ruler. Shadow puppeteers have used this for hundreds of years.

agreed.text: Each light makes its own shadow, so two lights make two shadows.
agreed.evidence: Switch on two torches and count the shadows. Switch one off, and one shadow goes.

agreed.text: Eclipses are shadows. In a lunar eclipse the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, and in a solar eclipse the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth.
agreed.evidence: Astronomers can work out exactly when the shadows will fall, years ahead, and the eclipses come on time.

challenging.claim: A shadow is a dark copy of you that follows you around.
challenging.who: An old idea in many lands, and a common first idea of young children
challenging.for: Your shadow has your shape, and it moves when you move.
challenging.against: Two lights give you two shadows. Your shadow grows and shrinks as you move nearer or further from the light. Switch the light off and it is gone at once. A copy of you would not double, grow or vanish like that.
challenging.context: This card is about what a shadow really is.

challenging.claim: A shadow is completely black, with no light in it at all.
challenging.for: Shadows look dark, especially next to bright light.
challenging.against: You can still see the floor inside a shadow. Light bounces off walls, ceilings and the sky into the shadow. Outdoors, shadows look a little blue, because light from the blue sky fills them.
challenging.context: This card is about what is inside a shadow.

challenging.claim: Clear glass makes no shadow at all.
challenging.for: Most light goes through clear glass, so you can see through it.
challenging.against: A glass tumbler of water makes a pale shadow with bright lines in it. Glass sends a little light back and bends some of it, so the patch behind it is not quite as bright.
challenging.context: This card is about shadows of see-through things.

challenging.claim: The black heron spreads her wings to make shade, so she can see the fish in the water.
challenging.who: Bird scientists who watch black herons in Africa
challenging.for: Shade cuts out the bright glare on the water, so it is easier to see into it.
challenging.against: Some scientists think the shade also tricks fish, because small fish swim into shady places to hide. It may do both jobs. Nobody is sure which matters more.
challenging.context: This card is about a bird who uses her own shadow to fish.

big_questions.q: When you step out of the light, where does your shadow go?
big_questions.hint: Did the shadow move away, or did the light just reach that place again?

big_questions.q: A shadow is made of missing light, yet you can draw round it and measure it. Is a shadow something, or nothing?
big_questions.hint: Think of the gap in a row of teeth. It is empty, yet you can see it and count it.

big_questions.q: Your toy made a small shadow and a giant one. Which one is the toy's real shadow?
big_questions.hint: Is there one right size for a shadow, or does it depend on where the toy and the light are?

big_questions.q: At night, your side of the Earth is turned away from the Sun. Is night a kind of shadow?
big_questions.hint: What blocks the Sun's light from you at night?

big_questions.q: A plant can sense the shade of a neighbour. Which other living beings might notice when your shadow falls over them?
big_questions.hint: Think of ants on the floor, a pigeon on the rail, or a cat asleep in the sun.

story.title: Paati's Lamp and the Growing Elephant
story.note: A made-up story. It is true that tholpavakoothu is a shadow-puppet play from the Palakkad area of Kerala, performed behind a white cloth lit by oil lamps, that it tells the Ramayana over many nights, and that a puppet's shadow grows as it moves towards the light.
text: Nila lived on the fifth floor of a tall building in Chennai, with her Amma, her Paati and her little brother Arjun. Nila was seven. Arjun was five. Paati was their grandmother. She had grown up in a village near Palakkad, in Kerala.
One evening in May, the fans stopped. The lights went out. The fridge went quiet. "Power cut," said Amma, and she went to find the torch.

Paati did not wait for the torch. She took out a small brass oil lamp, filled it with oil and lit the wick. She set it on the dining table, far from the curtains. A warm yellow flame stood up, still and bright.
Arjun gave a shout and grabbed Nila's arm. "Look! A giant!" On the wall behind Paati there was a huge dark head, with a bun on top, as tall as the door.

Paati laughed and moved her head. The giant moved its head too. "That giant is only my shadow," she said. "My head is in the way of the lamp. The light cannot get to that part of the wall, so it looks dark."
Arjun was not sure. He held his own hand up. A dark hand appeared on the wall. He wiggled his fingers, and the dark fingers wiggled. He hid his hand behind his back, and the dark hand was gone.
"Where did it go?" he asked.
"Nowhere," said Nila slowly. "It did not go anywhere. When your hand moved away, the light just reached the wall again."

Paati nodded. "When I was a girl," she said, "we walked to the temple at night to watch the tholpavakoothu. The puppeteers sat behind a long white cloth. Behind them was a row of little oil lamps, just like this one. They held leather puppets up between the lamps and the cloth. On our side, we saw only the shadows. Rama, Sita, Hanuman and the great king Ravana. They argued and sang and fought, night after night."
"Can we make one?" asked Nila.

Paati found an empty biscuit box. She drew an elephant on the card, with a long trunk and big ears. Nila cut it out carefully with the round-ended scissors. Paati made a small hole with a pencil for the eye, and they taped the elephant onto an ice-cream stick.
Arjun held the elephant up near the wall. A small, sharp elephant appeared, about the size of his hand. A tiny dot of light shone through the eye.
"It is only a baby elephant," said Arjun, disappointed.
"Try moving it," said Paati. "But keep it away from the flame."

Arjun stepped back towards the table, holding the elephant out in front of him. He stopped a long arm's length from the flame. The shadow on the wall grew. Its ears spread wide. Its trunk got longer and longer, until the elephant was taller than Amma, who had come back with the torch.
"It is growing!" Arjun shouted. "Is the elephant getting bigger?"
Nila looked at the card elephant in his hand. It was the same small elephant. Then she looked at the lamp. Its light spread out from the little flame, wider and wider, all the way to the wall.

"The elephant is not growing," said Nila. "When it is close to the lamp, it blocks a lot of the light. That missing light spreads all the way to the wall. So the dark patch is huge. When it is close to the wall, it only blocks a little bit."
Paati smiled. "Shadow puppeteers use the same trick," she said. "When Ravana comes on, angry and proud, they pull him back towards the lamps, and he fills the whole cloth."

Amma switched on the torch and shone it at the elephant from the other side of the room. Now there were two elephants on the wall, one from the lamp and one from the torch. Each one was grey, not black. Where they crossed, there was one dark patch.
"Two lights, two shadows," said Amma.
Arjun counted. "One elephant. Two shadows." He thought for a moment. "So the shadow belongs to the lamp, too. Not only to the elephant."
Then the fans whirred, and the tube light flickered on. The whole wall went bright. The elephant shadows went pale and nearly vanished.
"Oh," said Arjun. "The big light filled them in."
Paati blew out the little lamp. "Tomorrow," she said, "we will make Ravana. With ten heads."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Arjun first thinks the shadow is a thing that goes away and comes back, and that the elephant grows. Nila sees that the shadow is only the place the lamp's light cannot reach, so its size depends on where the puppet is. The second light shows Arjun that a shadow comes from the light and the puppet together.
ask: Where did Arjun's hand shadow go when he hid his hand?
Why did the elephant's shadow grow, when the card elephant stayed the same size?
Why were there two elephant shadows when Amma switched on the torch?
Why did the shadows nearly vanish when the tube light came on?

games.title: Shadow Challenge Cards
games.context: This is a game of shadow tricks. Each card asks you to make a shadow do something. You have to work out how, using what you know about light.

printables.title: 12 challenge cards to cut out, with a hint on the back

items.f: Make your hand's shadow bigger than your head.
items.b: Hint: move your hand close to the torch.

items.f: Make a shadow as small as a coin.
items.b: Hint: hold something small right next to the wall.

items.f: Make a shadow with a hole of light in it.
items.b: Hint: make a ring with your finger and thumb. Light goes through the hole.

items.f: Make a shadow with a sharp, crisp edge.
items.b: Hint: hold your hand close to the wall.

items.f: Make a shadow with a soft, fuzzy edge.
items.b: Hint: hold your hand close to the torch.

items.f: Make a shadow that points to the door.
items.b: Hint: put the torch on the side away from the door. The shadow falls on the far side.

items.f: Make a shadow vanish without moving the thing.
items.b: Hint: switch off the torch, or turn the torch away from the thing.

items.f: Make a round shadow with a steel plate.
items.b: Hint: hold the plate so its flat face looks at the torch.

items.f: Make a thin line shadow with the same steel plate.
items.b: Hint: turn the plate so its edge points at the torch.

items.f: Make two shadows of one spoon.
items.b: Hint: ask a grown-up to switch on a second light.

items.f: Make your hand's shadow reach the top of the wall.
items.b: Hint: put the torch low down, and bring your hand close to the torch.

items.f: Make a hand shadow with no gaps between the fingers.
items.b: Hint: hold your fingers tightly together, or make a fist.

rules: Close the curtains and make the room dim. One person holds the torch, or rests it on a pile of books pointing at a plain wall.
Put the cards in a pile with the challenge side up and the hint side down.
The first player takes the top card and reads it aloud, or someone reads it for them.
The player has one minute to make the shadow on the card. They may ask for the torch to be moved.
If everyone agrees the shadow was made, the player gets 2 points. If they needed to turn the card over and read the hint, they get 1 point.
Take turns until the pile is finished. The player with the most points wins. If points are equal, you all win.

setup.art: A dim room with a phone torch resting on a pile of books, pointing at a plain wall, and a pile of small paper cards on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Make the room dim. Point the torch at a plain wall.

setup.art: A girl reading a card, then holding her hand close to the torch while a huge hand shadow appears on the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card and make the shadow it asks for.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. 2. Find a steel plate, a spoon and a second light, such as a table lamp or another phone torch. 3. Make the room dim. 4. Rest the torch on a pile of books, pointing at a plain wall.
flow.say: Each of these cards asks for a shadow trick. You will need to think about where the light is.
flow.kid: Each card asks for a shadow trick. Think about where the light is.
flow.parent: Keep the room dim but not pitch dark, so nobody trips. A phone torch gives the sharpest shadows.

flow.do: 1. Players take turns to read a card and try it. 2. Give one minute for each card. 3. Write the points on the score sheet.
flow.say: Read your card. How will you do it? Tell us your plan first, then try it.
flow.kid: Read your card. Say your plan. Then try it.

ask.q: How did you make the shadow grow so big?
good: I put my hand near the torch.
Near the torch my hand blocks more light.

flow.parent: Let your child try their own idea first. Only point to the hint on the back if they are stuck after the minute.

flow.do: Add up the points. Then ask about the hardest card.
flow.say: Which card was the hardest? What did you find out from it?
flow.kid: Which card was hardest? What did you learn?

check.q: Kavya, a girl of 7, wants her hand's shadow to have a fuzzy edge. Where should she hold her hand?
check.why: Close to the torch, the bright part of the torch is partly hidden near the edge of the shadow, so the edge is grey and soft. Close to the wall, the edge is sharp. Behind the torch, there is no shadow on the wall at all.

games.title: Giant, Tiny, Gone!
games.players: 2 or more players. One of you is the caller.
games.context: This is a moving game. A caller shows a card, and the players must change their own shadows on the wall to match it, as fast as they can.

printables.title: 8 call cards to cut out, with what to do on the back

items.f: Giant!
items.b: Step close to the torch. Your shadow grows big.

items.f: Tiny!
items.b: Step close to the wall. Your shadow shrinks.

items.f: Gone!
items.b: Step out of the light. Your shadow disappears.

items.f: Sharp!
items.b: Stand close to the wall. The edge of your shadow gets crisp.

items.f: Fuzzy!
items.b: Stand close to the torch. The edge of your shadow goes soft.

items.f: Thin!
items.b: Turn sideways to the torch. Your shadow gets narrow.

items.f: Wide!
items.b: Face the torch and stretch your arms out. Your shadow gets wide.

items.f: Hide!
items.b: Stand right behind the caller, in the caller's shadow. Your own shadow joins theirs and seems to vanish.

rules: Put a torch on the floor at one end of a room, pointing at a plain wall about four big steps away.
The caller stands near the torch. The other players stand between the torch and the wall, where they can see their shadows.
The caller holds up the top card and reads it aloud.
The players change their shadows to match the card. The caller reads the back aloud to check.
The first player to get it right keeps the card and becomes the next caller. If nobody gets it right, the caller keeps the card.
The game ends when the cards run out. The player with the most cards wins.

setup.art: A torch on the floor of a living room pointing at a plain wall, and two children standing between the torch and the wall with big shadows.
setup.caption: 1. Torch on the floor, pointing at the wall. Players stand in between.

setup.art: A mother holding up a card that says 'Tiny!', and a girl running towards the wall while her shadow shrinks.
setup.caption: 2. The caller shows a card. Everyone changes their shadow.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 8 call cards. 2. Put the torch on the floor at one end of the room, pointing at a plain wall. 3. Move anything that people could trip on.
flow.say: Stand between the torch and the wall. Can you see your shadow? I will hold up a card. Change your shadow to match it.
flow.kid: Stand between the torch and the wall. Find your shadow. Watch for the card.
flow.parent: Clear the floor first, because players will rush back and forth in the dim light. Keep the room only dim, not fully dark.

flow.do: Hold up the cards one at a time, in any order. Read each one aloud.
flow.say: Giant! Tiny! Gone! Which way do you need to move? Why?
flow.kid: Watch the card. Move fast. Make your shadow match.

ask.q: To make your shadow giant, did you go towards the torch or the wall?
good: Towards the torch.
Near the torch, I block more of the light.

flow.parent: If a child goes the wrong way, let them look at their shadow and try again. They will soon feel the pattern.

flow.do: Sit down together and ask the question below. If the Hide! card did not come up, try it now.
flow.say: When you stood behind the caller, your shadow seemed to vanish. Where did it go?
flow.kid: When you hid behind the caller, where did your shadow go?

ask.q: Where did your shadow go when you hid behind the caller?
good: It was inside the caller's shadow.
No light reached me, so there was nothing to block.

flow.parent: A strong answer says that the caller was already blocking the light, so the child was standing in the dark and made no new shadow.

experiments.title: Near or Far: when does a shadow grow?
experiments.context: In this experiment you move one toy between a torch and a wall, and mark how tall its shadow is each time. You find out what changes the size of a shadow.
experiments.question: When a toy moves from the wall towards the torch, what happens to the size of its shadow?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Where will the toy's shadow be biggest: next to the wall, halfway, or next to the torch? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same toy, the same torch and the same wall each time. The torch stays in one place. Only the toy moves. We mark every shadow on the same paper, so we can compare them. We try each place twice, because one try can be a mistake.
results_table: My guess: small, middle or big?
How tall the shadow was (centimetres or finger widths)

materials.item: a small toy that stands up by itself, about as tall as your finger, such as a plastic animal or a doll
a torch, or a grown-up's phone with the torch on (a phone torch makes the sharpest shadows)
a table or the floor, next to a plain wall
two sheets of paper, taped one above the other on the wall, with the long sides upright
cellotape and a pencil
a ruler about 30 centimetres long, or your own fingers to count finger widths
three small paper strips, to mark the three places for the toy

schedule.what: Guess, set up the torch and paper, mark the toy's shadow at three places, measure, and talk about why.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Leave the three pencil marks on the paper, with a label next to each: wall, halfway, torch.

setup.art: A table pushed against a plain wall, two sheets of paper taped on the wall one above the other, starting at the table top, and a torch lying on its side about one metre away, pointing at the paper.
setup.caption: 1. Tape paper on the wall. Lay the torch about one metre away, pointing at it.

setup.art: Three paper strips on the table in a line between the torch and the wall: one half a ruler from the wall, one halfway, one a ruler's length from the torch.
setup.caption: 2. Mark three places: near the wall, halfway, near the torch.

setup.art: A small toy cow standing on the paper strip near the wall, with a small shadow on the paper, and a child's pencil marking the top of the shadow.
setup.caption: 3. Stand the toy at each place. Mark the top of its shadow.

setup.art: The paper on the wall with three pencil marks at different heights, labelled wall, halfway and torch, and a ruler held up against them.
setup.caption: 4. Measure each mark from the table top.

flow.do: 1. Draw the results table on paper, with three rows: near the wall, halfway, near the torch. 2. Show your child the toy. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason for each place.
flow.say: We will put this toy in three places between the torch and the wall. Where will its shadow be biggest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Where will the shadow be biggest? Near the wall, halfway, or near the torch? Why?

good: Near the wall, because the wall is where the shadow is.
Near the torch, because it blocks more light.
It will be the same, because the toy stays the same.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine if it has a reason. Many children guess the shadow stays the same size, because the toy does not change. Do not explain yet.

flow.do: 1. Push the table against a plain wall, or work on the floor next to the wall. 2. Tape the two sheets of paper on the wall, one above the other, starting at the table top. 3. Lay the torch on its side on the table, about one metre from the wall, pointing at the paper. 4. Close the curtains and switch off the room lights.
flow.say: This is our test track. The torch must stay exactly here the whole time. Why do you think that matters?
flow.kid: The torch stays in one place. Only the toy moves.
flow.parent: One metre is about two big steps for a child of 7. If you use a phone, prop it against a box so the torch on the back faces the wall. Evening is easiest, with the curtains closed. Keep the torch as low as the table top, so the shadows start at the table.

flow.do: 1. Put one paper strip half a ruler (about 15 centimetres) from the wall. 2. Put one halfway between the torch and the wall. 3. Put one a whole ruler (about 30 centimetres) from the torch. 4. All three go in a straight line between the torch and the wall.
flow.say: These strips are the three places for the toy. Let us put them in a straight line, so the shadow always lands on the paper.
flow.kid: Put the three strips in a line. Near the wall, halfway, near the torch.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands the toy on the strip near the wall. 2. They look at the shadow on the paper. 3. They make a pencil mark at the top of the shadow. 4. Write 'wall' next to the mark.
flow.say: Stand the toy near the wall. Look at its shadow. Put a small mark at the very top of the shadow.
flow.kid: Stand the toy near the wall. Mark the top of its shadow.
flow.parent: Your child must keep their own hand and head out of the light while they mark, or they will add their own shadow. Marking from the side works best.

flow.do: 1. Move the toy to the halfway strip, and mark the top of the shadow. Write 'halfway'. 2. Move it to the strip near the torch. Mark the top and write 'torch'. 3. Try each place a second time to check the marks.
flow.say: Now move the toy to halfway. Is the shadow changing? Now move it near the torch. What do you see? Look at the edge too.
flow.kid: Move the toy to halfway. Mark it. Then near the torch. Mark it. Look at the edge.

ask.q: What happened to the edge of the shadow near the torch?
good: It went fuzzy.
It was blurry, not sharp.

flow.parent: Near the torch the shadow is much taller, and its edge is soft. Mark the middle of the soft edge. If the shadow goes above the top sheet, tape on a third sheet.

flow.do: 1. Switch the room lights back on. 2. Measure each mark from the table top with a ruler, or count finger widths. 3. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Let us measure each mark. Which one is tallest? How many times taller is it than the one near the wall?
flow.kid: Measure each mark. Which is tallest? Write the numbers.
flow.parent: With a toy about 8 centimetres tall and the torch one metre from the wall, expect about 9 or 10 centimetres near the wall, about 16 halfway and about 27 near the torch. Your numbers will be different, but the pattern will be the same.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child what they think, what they saw, and why. Then read the card Nearer the light, bigger shadow.
flow.say: Was your guess right? The toy never changed size. So why did its shadow grow?
flow.kid: Was your guess right? The toy stayed the same. Why did the shadow grow?

ask.q: Why was the shadow biggest near the torch?
good: Near the torch, the toy blocks more of the light.
The light spreads out, so the blocked part gets bigger on the way to the wall.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the marks: 'Near the wall the shadow was 10 centimetres, near the torch it was 30. The toy blocked more of the light near the torch.'

check.q: Meenakshi, a girl of 7, wants a giant shadow of her small toy horse. Where should she put the horse?
check.why: Close to the torch, the horse blocks a big part of the spreading light, so the shadow on the wall is big. If you picked the wall, try the test again and watch the shadow shrink as the toy moves to the wall.

experiments.title: Two Lights: how many shadows?
experiments.context: In this experiment you shine two lights on one toy at the same time. You count the shadows and look at how dark each one is.
experiments.question: If two lights shine on one toy from different places, how many shadows will it make, and how dark will they be?
experiments.predict: Guess first. With two lights on, will the toy have one shadow, two shadows, or none? Will they be darker or paler than with one light? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same toy in the same place the whole time. We keep each light in the same spot. We change only which lights are switched on, so we know what made each change.

materials.item: two torches, or two phones with their torches on, or one torch and a table lamp
a small toy that stands up by itself
a table or the floor next to a plain wall
a pencil and the results table on paper

schedule.what: Guess, then try light A alone, both lights, and light B alone. Count the shadows and fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw what the wall looked like with both lights on.

setup.art: A toy standing on a table near a plain wall, with two torches on piles of books about a hand-span apart, both pointing at the toy.
setup.caption: 1. Two lights, a hand-span apart, both pointing at the toy.

setup.art: The wall behind the toy showing two pale grey toy shadows side by side, overlapping a little in a darker patch.
setup.caption: 2. Switch both on. Count the shadows.

setup.art: One torch switched off, and only one shadow on the wall, now darker.
setup.caption: 3. Switch one light off. Which shadow goes?

flow.do: 1. Draw the results table with three rows: light A only, both lights, light B only. 2. Ask your child to guess, with a reason.
flow.say: We have one toy and two lights. When both lights are on, how many shadows will the toy have? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One toy. Two lights. How many shadows? Why?

good: One, because there is one toy.
Two, because each light makes a shadow.
None, because the second light will light up the shadow.

flow.parent: All three guesses are common. Do not say which is right.

flow.do: 1. Stand the toy on a table, a hand-span from a plain wall. 2. Put light A on a pile of books, a big step from the toy, pointing at it. 3. Put light B a hand-span to one side of light A, also pointing at the toy. 4. Make the room dark.
flow.say: Let us set up both lights. They must both point at the toy, but from different places.
flow.kid: Two lights. Both point at the toy, from different places.
flow.parent: If you use phones, a grown-up handles them. A table lamp works as one of the lights if you take off the shade.

flow.do: 1. Switch on light A only. 2. Your child counts the shadows and says how dark the shadow is. 3. Write it in the table.
flow.say: Light A only. How many shadows? Is it dark or pale?
flow.kid: Light A only. How many shadows? Dark or pale?

flow.do: 1. Switch on light B as well. 2. Your child counts the shadows. 3. They look at where the shadows overlap. 4. Write it in the table.
flow.say: Now both lights. How many shadows? Are they as dark as before? Look where they cross.
flow.kid: Both lights on. Count the shadows. Look where they cross.
flow.parent: You should see two shadows, each a paler grey than before. Where they overlap, it is dark. If the shadows are on top of each other, move one light a little further to the side. If they do not touch at all, move the lights closer together or the toy closer to the wall.

flow.do: 1. Switch off light A, so only light B is on. 2. Your child says which shadow went away, and whether the other got darker. 3. Write it in the table.
flow.say: I am switching off light A. Which shadow went away? What happened to the other one?
flow.kid: Light A is off. Which shadow went? Did the other get darker?

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child what they think, what they saw, and why. Then read the card Two lights, two shadows.
flow.say: How many shadows did the toy have with two lights? Why was each one paler than with one light?
flow.kid: How many shadows with two lights? Why were they paler?

ask.q: Why were the two shadows pale grey and not dark?
good: The other light shone on each shadow.
Light A lit up light B's shadow.

flow.parent: A strong answer: 'Two shadows, one from each light. Each one was pale, because the other light still shone there. Where they crossed, no light got in, so it was dark.'

check.q: Jonali in Guwahati has a tube light and a table lamp on in her room. How many shadows does her chair make on the floor?
check.why: Each light makes its own shadow, so two lights make two shadows. If you picked one, try your test again with both lights on, and count.

activities.title: Make a Shadow, Lose a Shadow
activities.context: In this activity you make a hand shadow with a torch. Then you try three ways to make it disappear. You find out what a shadow needs.

materials.item: a torch, or a grown-up's phone with the torch on
a room you can make dim, with a plain wall

schedule.what: Make a hand shadow, then make it vanish in three ways.

activities.record: Draw the three things a shadow needs: a light, a hand and a wall.

setup.art: A child holding a hand between a torch and a plain wall, with a dark hand shadow on the wall.
setup.caption: 1. Hold your hand between the torch and the wall.

setup.art: Three small pictures: the torch switched off, the hand moved away, and the torch pointing out of an open window at the night sky.
setup.caption: 2. Try three ways to lose the shadow.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dim. 2. A grown-up points the torch at a plain wall. 3. Your child holds one hand between the torch and the wall.
flow.say: Hold your hand in front of the torch. What do you see on the wall?
flow.kid: Hold your hand in front of the torch. What is on the wall?
flow.parent: Let your child play with the hand shadow for a moment before asking anything.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to find a way to make the shadow vanish. 2. Then a second way. 3. Then a third way. Give hints only if they are stuck.
flow.say: Can you make the shadow disappear? Find a way. Now find another way. Is there a third way?
flow.kid: Make the shadow vanish. Then find another way. And another.

good: Switching off the torch.
Taking my hand away.
Pointing the torch where there is no wall.

flow.parent: The three ways are: switch off the light, take away the hand, or take away the wall by pointing the torch out of an open window at the night sky. Some children also hide the hand behind the torch, which is the same as taking it away from the light. Stay beside your child at the window and keep them back from the edge or grill.

flow.do: Ask your child to name what a shadow needs.
flow.say: So what does a shadow need? How many things?
flow.kid: What does a shadow need? Count them on your fingers.

check.q: Lakshmi, a girl of 7, switches off the torch. What happens to her hand shadow?
options: It stays on the wall for a while
check.why: A shadow is the place light cannot reach. With the torch off, no light reaches the wall at all, so there is no dark patch to see. The shadow is gone at once.

activities.title: Make a Card Shadow Puppet
activities.context: In this activity you cut a shadow puppet from an old box and put it on a stick. You find out which parts show up in the shadow, and how to give your puppet a shining eye.

materials.item: thin card from an old box, such as a biscuit or cereal box
a pencil
scissors, used with a grown-up
an ice-cream stick, a straw or a pencil, for the handle
cellotape
a torch and a plain wall

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the eye hole with a pencil point and helps with the scissors.

schedule.what: Draw, cut and tape a puppet, then try it in front of the torch.

activities.record: Draw your puppet and its shadow side by side. Colour the puppet, and leave the shadow dark.

setup.art: A child drawing a crow shape on the plain side of an opened-out biscuit box.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a big, simple animal on the card.

setup.art: A grown-up and a child cutting out the crow, with a small hole poked for the eye.
setup.caption: 2. Cut it out. Poke a hole for the eye.

setup.art: The card crow taped to an ice-cream stick, held in front of a torch, with a crow shadow on the wall and a dot of light for the eye.
setup.caption: 3. Tape it to a stick. Hold it in the light.

flow.do: 1. Open out an old box and use the plain inside. 2. Your child draws a big animal outline, about as big as their hand. 3. Choose an animal with a clear shape, such as a crow, an elephant, a fish or a cat.
flow.say: Draw an animal as big as your hand. Make the outline clear, with a beak, a trunk or a tail that sticks out. Why do you think the outline matters?
flow.kid: Draw a big animal. Give it a clear outline.
flow.parent: A shadow shows only the outline, so shapes with a trunk, ears, a beak or a tail work best. Colours and faces drawn inside will not show.

flow.do: 1. Help your child cut along the outline. 2. Poke a small hole for the eye with a sharp pencil. 3. Tape the stick to the back, at the bottom.
flow.say: Let us cut along your line. Now we make a hole for the eye. What do you think the hole will look like in the shadow?
flow.kid: Cut along the line. Make a hole for the eye. What will the hole look like?
flow.parent: Help with tight corners like a beak. Make the hole yourself with the pencil point, pushing into a folded cloth or an eraser behind the card.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dim. 2. Your child holds the puppet between the torch and the wall. 3. Ask them to look at the colours, the eye and the outline.
flow.say: Hold your puppet in the light. Which parts show in the shadow? Did the colours show? What about the eye?
flow.kid: Hold up your puppet. Which parts show in the shadow? What about the eye?

ask.q: Why does the eye show as a dot of light?
good: Light goes through the hole.
The card blocks the light, but the hole lets it through.

flow.parent: Your child sees that the colours do not show, only the outline, and that the eye hole makes a bright dot.

flow.do: Ask your child to make the puppet move, grow and shrink.
flow.say: Can you make your puppet walk? Can you make it grow huge, then shrink?
flow.kid: Make your puppet walk. Make it grow. Make it shrink.
flow.think: If you cut a mouth hole too, what would the shadow look like?

activities.title: Which Way Does It Point?
activities.context: In this activity you move a torch all round a toy and watch where the shadow falls. You find out how to tell where a light is from its shadow.

materials.item: a small toy or a steel tumbler
a big sheet of paper or an old newspaper, laid on the floor
a torch
a pencil

schedule.what: Shine the torch from four sides and from above, and draw each shadow.

activities.record: On the paper, the toy's spot in the middle, with four shadow drawings round it and an arrow showing where the torch was for each.

setup.art: A toy standing in the middle of a sheet of paper on the floor, with a torch on the paper to the left of it, low down, and a shadow stretching to the right.
setup.caption: 1. Torch on one side, low down. Draw the shadow.

setup.art: The same toy with four pencil shadows drawn round it, pointing four ways, each with a small torch drawn on the opposite side.
setup.caption: 2. Move the torch round. The shadow swings round too.

flow.do: 1. Lay the paper on the floor and stand the toy in the middle. 2. Make the room dim. 3. Lay the torch on the paper, low down, on one side of the toy, pointing at it. Prop it on a small book to keep it still. 4. Your child draws round the shadow.
flow.say: The torch is low, here on this side. Where is the shadow? Draw round it.
flow.kid: The torch is low on one side. Draw round the shadow.

flow.do: 1. Before each move, ask your child to guess where the shadow will go. 2. Move the torch to the other three sides in turn, and prop it to keep it still. 3. Draw each shadow, and an arrow showing where the torch was.
flow.say: Before you move the torch, guess: where will the shadow go now? Why?
flow.kid: Guess where the shadow will go. Then move the torch and see.

ask.q: Where will the shadow go if the torch is in front?
good: Behind the toy.
On the far side, away from the torch.

flow.do: Hold the torch straight above the toy, pointing down. Ask what happened to the shadow.
flow.say: Now the torch is high above the toy. Where is the shadow? Is it long or short?
flow.kid: Torch high up. Where is the shadow now? Long or short?
flow.parent: With the light straight above, the shadow becomes short and sits round the bottom of the toy, like the shadow under a chair from a ceiling light.

check.q: Farhan holds the torch on the left of his toy. Where does the shadow fall?
options: On the right of the toy
On the left of the toy
check.why: A shadow always falls on the side away from the light. The torch is on the left, so the shadow is on the right.

activities.title: Draw a Shadow Portrait
activities.context: In this activity a family member sits side-on to a torch, and you trace the shadow of their face on paper. The outline is called a silhouette, and you can tell who it is from the outline alone.

materials.item: a big sheet of paper or chart paper, taped on a wall
a torch on a pile of books, or a table lamp with the shade taken off
a pencil and a black crayon
a chair

schedule.what: Seat someone side-on, trace their shadow, then colour it in.

activities.record: The finished shadow portrait, with the person's name written underneath.

setup.art: A grandmother sitting side-on on a chair close to a wall with paper on it, and a torch on books shining on her from the other side, making a clear side-face shadow.
setup.caption: 1. Sit side-on, close to the wall. Light from the other side.

setup.art: A girl tracing round the shadow of her grandmother's face with a pencil.
setup.caption: 2. Trace round the shadow.

setup.art: A finished black side-face picture on white paper, with a hair bun, on the wall.
setup.caption: 3. Colour it in dark.

flow.do: 1. Tape the paper on the wall at head height for someone sitting. 2. Seat the person side-on, close to the wall. 3. Put the light on the other side, about two big steps away, at the same height as their head.
flow.say: Who shall we draw? Sit close to the wall, sideways. Why do you think they should sit close to the wall?
flow.kid: Pick someone to draw. They sit sideways, close to the wall.
flow.parent: Sitting close to the wall makes the shadow sharp and about the same size as the real face. The person must keep very still for about two minutes.

flow.do: 1. Your child traces round the shadow with a pencil. 2. Move the light a little if your child's own shadow gets in the way. 3. Then colour the inside dark.
flow.say: Trace round the shadow slowly, keeping out of the light. Can you get the nose and the chin?
flow.kid: Trace round the shadow slowly. Keep out of the light.
flow.parent: Your child will find their own hand makes a shadow too. Tracing from the side, with the hand low, helps.

flow.do: Show the portrait to someone who did not watch it being made. Ask them to guess who it is.
flow.say: Can someone who did not watch guess who this is from the outline alone? What gives it away?
flow.kid: Can someone guess who it is? What gives it away?

ask.q: How can you tell who it is, with no eyes or colours?
good: The shape of the nose.
The hair bun.
The chin and the glasses.

activities.title: Shadow Hunt at Home
activities.context: In this activity you look for shadows all round your home, in daylight and at night. You count how many shadows a thing has, and find the light that made each one.

materials.item: a pencil and paper for a tally

schedule.what: Walk round your home, find shadows, and find the light for each.

activities.record: A list of the shadows you found, with the light that made each one, and how many shadows the most-shadowed thing had.

setup.art: A child crouching to look at the shadow under a dining table, pointing up at the ceiling light.
setup.caption: 1. Find a shadow. Point to the light that made it.

setup.art: A chair in a room with a tube light and a lamp on, and two shadows of the chair on the floor, with tally marks on a paper.
setup.caption: 2. Count how many shadows one thing has.

flow.do: 1. Walk round the home with your child. 2. For each shadow you find, ask your child to point to the light that made it. 3. Make a tally mark for each shadow.
flow.say: Find a shadow. Now point to the light that made it. How do you know it was that light?
flow.kid: Find a shadow. Point to its light. Make a tally mark.

ask.q: How do you know which light made that shadow?
good: The shadow points away from it.
When I cover the light, the shadow goes.

flow.do: 1. At night, switch on two or three lights in one room. 2. Ask your child to find the thing with the most shadows. 3. Count its shadows together.
flow.say: Which thing in this room has the most shadows? How many? Why so many?
flow.kid: Find the thing with the most shadows. Count them. Why so many?
flow.parent: With two or more lights on, chairs and people have one shadow for each light. If sunlight comes in through a window in the day, look at the shadows it makes on the floor too.

projects.title: Our Box Theatre Shadow Play
projects.context: In this project you build a small shadow theatre from a cardboard box, make three puppets, and put on a short play for your family, like a tholpavakoothu play from Kerala.

materials.item: a big cardboard box, such as a delivery carton
white paper, butter paper, or a thin old white cotton cloth, for the screen
thin card from old boxes, for the puppets
ice-cream sticks, straws or pencils, for handles
cellotape, a pencil and scissors used with a grown-up
a torch or a grown-up's phone with the torch on

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the window in the box, because cardboard needs a sharp blade or strong scissors.

schedule.what: Build the box theatre with its screen, choose a story, and draw and cut three puppets.
Practise the play with the torch behind the screen, then perform it for the family.

projects.record: A drawing or photo of the box theatre, and the names of the three puppets and the story you told.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting a big rectangle out of the bottom of a cardboard box, and taping white butter paper over the hole.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a window in a box. Cover it with white paper.

setup.art: Three card puppets on sticks: a crow, a clay pot and a handful of pebbles.
setup.caption: 2. Make three puppets on sticks.

setup.art: A child behind the box with a phone torch shining from behind, holding a crow puppet against the paper, and the family in front watching a crow shadow on the glowing screen.
setup.caption: 3. Light from behind. The audience watches from the front.

flow.do: 1. Stand the box on its side, open end towards you. 2. Cut a big window in the far side, leaving a border of about two fingers. 3. Tape white paper or thin white cloth over the window.
flow.say: This will be our theatre. The paper is the screen. Where do you think the light should go: in front of the screen, or behind it?
flow.kid: This box is our theatre. Where should the light go? In front, or behind?
flow.parent: The light goes behind the screen, with the puppets between the light and the screen. The audience sits in front and sees only shadows.

flow.do: 1. Choose a short story with three characters, such as The Thirsty Crow. 2. Your child draws three puppets on card. 3. Cut them out and tape on the stick handles.
flow.say: Which story shall we tell? Who are the three characters? Draw each one with a clear outline.
flow.kid: Pick a story. Draw three puppets with clear outlines.
flow.parent: In The Thirsty Crow, a crow drops pebbles into a pot until the water rises high enough to drink. The three puppets are a crow, a pot and some pebbles. Only outlines show, so add holes for eyes or for water in the pot.

flow.do: 1. On day 2, put the torch on a pile of books about one big step behind the box. 2. Your child holds a puppet between the torch and the screen. 3. Look at the shadow from the front together.
flow.say: Hold the crow close to the screen. Now pull it back towards the torch. What happens to the crow's shadow?
flow.kid: Hold the puppet near the screen. Pull it back to the torch. Watch the shadow.

ask.q: How can you make the crow look like they are flying far away?
good: Hold the puppet close to the screen, so the shadow gets small and sharp.
Move it away from the torch.

flow.parent: Close to the screen the shadow is small and sharp. Pulled back towards the torch, it grows big and fuzzy. Puppeteers use this to make a character arrive or seem huge.

flow.do: 1. Practise the story once. 2. Gather the family in front, and switch off the room lights. 3. Your child performs the play.
flow.say: Our show is about to start. Tell the story in your own words while you move the puppets.
flow.kid: Tell the story. Move the puppets. Enjoy the show!
flow.parent: Afterwards, let the audience ask the puppeteer one question about how the shadows were made.

challenges.title: Build a Shadow Monster
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a monster from kitchen things, but only its shadow will be seen. Your job is to make the shadow look as amazing as you can.
challenges.problem: Can you build a monster from kitchen things whose shadow has a big head, glowing eyes and claws, and can grow huge on the wall?
constraints: Use only things from the kitchen that will not break, such as spoons, forks, a tea strainer, a paper plate and steel plates, plus tape.
The shadow must have at least two eyes of light.
Someone must be able to make the monster's shadow grow and shrink.
materials: a pencil to poke holes, used by a grown-up
a torch and a plain wall
general: Use a paper plate for the head, with two holes poked for glowing eyes.
Tape forks to the sides as claws. Their prongs show as sharp spikes in the shadow.
Move the monster close to the torch to make it grow, and back to the wall to shrink it.
creative: Hold a tea strainer in front for a head full of tiny dots of light. A very fine mesh makes only a pale, speckled patch, so try a coarser one.
Switch on a second light to give the monster two shadows, like twin monsters.
Move the torch while the monster stays still, so the shadow seems to walk.
challenges.your_turn: Build your own monster. Does its shadow have glowing eyes? Can you make it grow? If a part does not show, turn it so its outline faces the torch, and try again.

opts: A dark patch where light is blocked
A dark copy that comes out of a thing
quiz.why: A shadow is the place the light cannot reach, because something is in the way. Nothing dark comes out of the thing.

quiz.p: Kavya wants to make a shadow on her bedroom wall. Which of these does she NOT need?
quiz.why: A shadow needs a light, something to block it, and a surface for the shadow to fall on. A mirror is not needed.

quiz.p: In the Near or Far test, where was the toy's shadow biggest?
opts: When the toy was close to the torch
When the toy was close to the wall
It was the same size everywhere
quiz.why: Close to the torch, the toy blocks a big part of the spreading light, so the shadow on the wall is big.

quiz.p: A torch shines on a doll from the right. Where is the doll's shadow?
opts: On the left of the doll
On the right of the doll
quiz.why: A shadow falls on the side away from the light. The light comes from the right, so the shadow is on the left.

quiz.p: A lamp hangs straight above a dining table. Where is the table's shadow?
opts: On the wall behind the lamp
quiz.why: The light comes from above, so the blocked place is below the table, on the floor.

quiz.p: With two torches on, why is each shadow pale grey, not dark?
opts: The other torch still shines into it
quiz.why: Each shadow is lit by the other torch. Only where the two shadows overlap does no light get in, so that part is dark.

quiz.p: Your shadow puppet is a crow coloured bright blue. What colour is the crow's shadow?
quiz.why: The card blocks the light, so the shadow is dark. A shadow shows only the outline, not the colours painted on the card.

quiz.p: Tholpavakoothu is a shadow-puppet play from which state?
quiz.why: Tholpavakoothu comes from Kerala, mostly round Palakkad. Andhra Pradesh has tholu bommalata, Karnataka has togalu gombeyaata and Odisha has ravanachhaya.

quiz.p: Why does a shadow have the same outline as the thing that makes it?
quiz.why: Light that just misses the edge goes straight on to the wall, and light that hits the thing stops. So the edge of the shadow follows the edge of the thing.

quiz.p: Revathi holds her hand very close to the torch. What does the edge of the shadow look like?
quiz.why: Close to the torch, the edge of the shadow gets a little light from part of the torch, so it is grey and soft. Close to the wall, the edge is sharp.

items.p: Which three things do you need to make a shadow?
opts: A light, something to block it, and a surface
A light, a mirror, and some water
items.why: A strong answer names all three: a light, something to block the light, and a wall or floor for the shadow to fall on.
items.art: A torch, a hand and a wall, drawn small.

items.p: True or false: a toy's shadow falls on the side of the toy away from the torch.
items.why: True. The light stops at the toy, so the place behind it, away from the torch, gets no light.

items.p: Draw a torch, a ball and a wall. Then draw where the ball's shadow falls, and colour it dark.
items.a: A torch on one side, the ball in the middle, and a round dark shadow on the wall behind the ball.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the shadow on the wall on the far side of the ball from the torch, in a straight line with them.

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to the shape of its shadow.
pairs: a steel plate, flat face to the torch
a book, front cover to the torch
a fork, flat face to the torch
items.why: A shadow has the outline of the thing, as seen from the torch.

items.p: A shadow is the dark patch where light is ___.
items.why: Something is in the way, so the light cannot reach that patch.

items.p: Remember the Near or Far test. Say it, and a grown-up writes it down: why did your toy's shadow grow when it was near the torch?
items.a: Near the torch, the toy blocked more of the light, so the dark patch on the wall was bigger.
items.why: A strong answer says the toy stayed the same size, and that near the torch it blocked a bigger part of the spreading light.

items.p: Label the picture: torch, light, toy, shadow, wall.
a: torch: where the light comes from
light: the yellow lines from the torch
toy: the thing in the way
shadow: the dark patch on the wall
items.why: These are the parts of every shadow: a light, the light itself, a blocker, the shadow and a surface.
items.art: A torch on the left, yellow lines of light, a toy in the middle and a wall on the right with a dark toy shadow.

items.p: Sort these into: makes a dark shadow, or makes only a very pale shadow.
items.why: Opaque things like steel, books and hands block the light, so they make dark shadows. Clear glass and clear polythene let most light through.

items.p: Look at the picture. Three toys stand in a row on a table, and one torch shines on all of them. How many shadows are on the wall?
items.why: Each toy blocks the light of the torch, so each toy has its own shadow. One torch and three toys make three shadows.
items.art: Three small toys in a row on a table, one lit torch on one side, and three grey toy shadows on the wall.

items.p: Put the toy's shadows in order, from the smallest to the biggest.
items: the toy close to the torch
the toy close to the wall
a: the toy close to the wall
the toy close to the torch
items.why: The nearer the toy is to the torch, the more light it blocks, so the bigger its shadow.

items.p: Lakshmi holds her puppet close to the wall. Its shadow is small and sharp. What happens if she moves it towards the lamp?
opts: The shadow gets bigger and fuzzier
The shadow gets smaller and sharper
items.why: Moving towards the lamp, the puppet blocks more of the spreading light, so the shadow grows. Its edge also gets fuzzy.

items.p: Three friends are arguing about a shadow.

views.says: A shadow belongs to the puppet. It has the puppet's shape.
A shadow belongs to the light. With two lights, one puppet makes two shadows.
A shadow needs the puppet and the light together. Take either away, and it is gone.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason from your own tests. Then say one thing another friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses evidence. Kavya is right that the outline comes from the puppet. Farhan is right that each light makes its own shadow. Meena is right that both are needed.
items.why: A shadow's shape comes from the blocker, but its place, size and number come from the light. Every view sees part of it.

items.p: Remember the Two Lights test. Why did one toy have two shadows?
items.a: Each light made its own shadow, because the toy blocked some light from each one.
items.why: A strong answer says one shadow came from each light, and may add that switching one light off made its shadow go.

items.p: Draw a puppet with a hole for the eye. Next to it, draw its shadow on the wall. Show what the eye looks like in the shadow.
items.a: A dark puppet shadow with a bright dot where the eye hole is.
items.why: The card blocks the light, but the hole lets light through, so the eye shows as a bright dot in the dark shadow.
items.art: An empty box split into two halves: puppet, and shadow.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? A lit diya, the Sun, a tube light, the Moon.
items.why: A diya, the Sun and a tube light give out their own light, so they are light sources. The Moon gives out none. We see the Moon because sunlight bounces off it.

items.p: True or false: a shadow can fall on the ceiling.
items.why: True. A shadow falls wherever something blocks the light and a surface is there. Hold your hand above a torch that points up, and its shadow falls on the ceiling.

items.p: Light travels in ___ lines, so it cannot bend round the toy.
items.why: Because light goes in straight lines, the edge of the shadow follows the edge of the toy.

items.p: Sai sees his shadow on the floor pointing towards the door. Where is the light?
opts: On the side away from the door
items.why: A shadow points away from the light. So if the shadow points to the door, the light is on the other side, away from the door.

items.p: Many people think a shadow is completely black. In your tests, could you still see the floor or wall inside a shadow? Why?
items.a: Yes. Some light bounces off the walls and ceiling into the shadow, so it is dark grey, not totally black.
items.why: A strong answer uses what the child saw. Light bounces off the walls, the ceiling and other things into the shadow.

items.p: Label the picture of a big shadow: the dark middle, and the fuzzy edge.
a: dark middle: where no light from the torch gets in
fuzzy edge: where a little light from part of the torch still gets in
items.why: The fuzzy edge is grey because part of the torch's bright face can still be seen from there.
items.art: A big hand shadow with a dark middle and a soft grey edge all round it.

items.p: In Africa, a bird called the black heron spreads her wings like an umbrella over the water while she fishes. Three people give a reason.

views.says: The shade cuts the bright glare on the water, so she can see the fish.

views.who: Thenmozhi, a girl who watches birds
views.says: Small fish like to hide in shady places, so they swim into her shadow.
It does both jobs at once.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. Dr Asha is right that shade makes it easier to see into water. Thenmozhi is right that many small fish hide in shade. Gauri may be right too. Scientists still argue about this.
items.why: This is a real question that scientists are still studying, so more than one answer can be well argued.

items.p: Hetal, a girl in Class 2, wants the shadow of her toy to be almost the same size as the toy. Where should she hold it? Why?
items.a: As close to the wall as she can, because there the toy blocks only a small part of the spreading light, so the shadow is about the same size as the toy.
items.why: A strong answer gives the place and says the shadow grows as the toy moves towards the torch, so near the wall it stays small.

items.p: Draw the shadow of a steel tumbler standing up, when a torch shines at it from the side. Then draw its shadow when the tumbler lies on its side with the open end facing the torch.
items.a: Standing: a rectangle, a little wider at the top. Lying with the open end to the torch: a circle.
items.why: A shadow shows the outline of a thing as seen from the light. A standing tumbler seen from the side looks like a rectangle. Seen from its open end, it looks round.
items.art: An empty box split into two halves: standing, and lying down.

items.p: In a long school corridor, there is a light on the ceiling every few steps. What do you see as you walk along?
opts: Several shadows of you, one from each nearby light
Exactly one shadow, always in front
items.why: Each light makes its own shadow, so you have several shadows, and they change as you walk past each light.

items.p: A shadow is made of missing light. Yet in the Near or Far test you measured it with a ruler. How did you measure something made of missing light?
items.a: I marked where the dark patch ended at the top and measured from the table to the mark. The edge of the shadow is where the light starts again.
items.why: A strong answer says you measure where the light stops and starts. The edge is real, even if the patch is only missing light.

items.p: True or false: a plant can sense the shade of other leaves, and grow taller to get out of it.
items.why: True. Light under leaves has less red light. Plants sense this and grow longer stems to reach sunlight.

items.p: Draw a line from each shadow-puppet play to the state it comes from.
items.why: India has shadow plays in many states, each with its own name, puppets and stories.

items.p: Sort these into: gives a sharper shadow, or gives a fuzzier shadow.
items: a big window on a cloudy day
the toy close to the wall
the toy close to the torch
items.why: Small lights and things close to the wall give sharp shadows. Big lights, like a whole cloudy sky, and things close to the light give fuzzy edges.

items.p: Put these steps for a box theatre shadow play in order.
items: Hold the puppets between the torch and the screen
Cut a window in a box and cover it with white paper
Put the torch behind the box
a: Cut a window in a box and cover it with white paper
Put the torch behind the box
Hold the puppets between the torch and the screen
items.why: First the screen, then the puppets, then the light behind, and last the puppets go between the light and the screen.

items.p: Four children stand in a room with two lamps on. How many shadows of children are there?
items.why: Each child has one shadow from each lamp, so 2 each. Four children with 2 shadows each make 8.

applications: Shadow-puppet plays in Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Odisha tell long stories with leather puppets, lamps and a white cloth.
Umbrellas, sun hats, shade nets and trees block sunlight to keep people and other animals cool.
Plant nurseries in India grow young plants under green shade nets, which block part of the strong sunlight.
An X-ray picture is a kind of shadow picture. Bones block more X-rays than the soft parts do, so they show up pale.

spotted.text: At lunch, look under the dining table. The ceiling light makes a dark shadow on the floor.
spotted.art: A family eating lunch at a dining table, with a dark patch on the floor under the table.

spotted.text: In a tholpavakoothu play in Palakkad, the shadows of leather puppets move on a long white cloth lit by oil lamps.
spotted.art: A white cloth screen glowing at night, with the shadow of Hanuman leaping across it.

spotted.text: Walking at night past a street light, your shadow is short when you are close to the pole and gets longer as you walk away.
spotted.art: A girl walking past a street light on a road at night, with a long shadow stretching ahead of her.

spotted.text: On a hot afternoon, people wait for the bus in the shade of a banyan tree or a bus shelter.

open_questions.q: Did shadow-puppet plays begin in India, in China, or somewhere else?
open_questions.why_open: Shadow plays are very old in India, China and South-East Asia. Old written records are few, so historians still argue about where the first ones were.

open_questions.q: How does a plant weigh up a neighbour's shade against everything else they sense?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know plants sense shade with light-sensing proteins. How a plant puts this together with water, touch and the seasons to decide how to grow is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: What exactly did the Mohists write about shadows?
open_questions.why_open: Their book was copied by hand for many centuries, and parts were damaged or muddled. Scholars still argue about how to read some of the notes.

maths.problem: In a Near or Far test, a toy's shadow was 10 centimetres tall near the wall and 30 centimetres tall near the torch. How many times taller was the shadow near the torch?
maths.explain: Count in tens: 10, 20, 30. That is three tens. So 30 centimetres is 3 times 10 centimetres.
maths.context: This is about the Near or Far test, where you moved a toy between a torch and a wall.
maths.why_maths: Saying '3 times taller' tells us how much bigger the shadow got, not just that it got bigger.

maths.problem: Three puppets stand in a room with two lamps on. Each puppet has one shadow from each lamp. How many shadows are there in all?
maths.explain: Each puppet has 2 shadows. Three puppets: 2, 4, 6. So there are 6 shadows.
maths.context: This is about the Two Lights test, where one toy made two shadows.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal groups tells us how many shadows to expect before we look.

maths.problem: Three shadows of the same toy were 14 centimetres, 9 centimetres and 31 centimetres tall. Put them in order from smallest to biggest. Which one was the toy close to the torch?
maths.answer: 9, 14, 31. The 31 centimetre shadow was the toy close to the torch.
maths.explain: 9 is the smallest, then 14, then 31. The nearer the toy is to the torch, the bigger its shadow, so the biggest one, 31, was nearest the torch.
maths.context: This is about the Near or Far test, with made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Putting the numbers in order lets us match each shadow to where the toy stood.

maths.problem: Nila folds a card in half and cuts out half a butterfly along the fold. When she opens it, both wings match. Will the butterfly's shadow have matching wings too? Why?
maths.answer: Yes. The shadow has the same outline as the card, so its two halves match as well.
maths.explain: The fold is a line of symmetry. A shadow keeps the outline of the card, so the shadow has the same line of symmetry.
maths.context: This is about making card shadow puppets.
maths.why_maths: Symmetry helps us cut a puppet with two matching sides in one go, and predict its shadow.

maths.problem: The family's shadow play started at 7 o'clock in the evening and lasted half an hour. At what time did it end?
maths.explain: Half an hour after 7 o'clock, the long hand has moved half way round the clock, to the 6. That is half past 7.
maths.context: This is about the box theatre shadow play.
maths.why_maths: Knowing the time it ends helps the family plan the show before dinner.
